model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Checkers on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(my_men, my_kings, opp_men, opp_kings, color) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `my_men` is a list of squares containing your regular pieces. - `my_kings` is a list of squares containing your kings. - `opp_men` is a list of squares containing opponent regular pieces. - `opp_kings` is a list of squares containing opponent kings. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which moves downwards (to lower row values) and `'w'` for white which moves upwards (to higher row values). - Squares use coordinates: row `0`-`7`, column `0`-`7`. - `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left corner; rows increase bottom-to-top and columns increase left-to-right. - Only dark squares are playable. # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a tuple: `((from_row, from_col), (to_row, to_col))`. - `from_row`, `to_row`, `from_col`, `to_col` are coordinates `0..7`. - (`from_row`, `from_col`) has to be a coordinate of a piece that is yours and (`to_row`, `to_col`) has to be the destination square.Return a legal move; captures are mandatory when available. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm working through standard English draughts rules — men capture diagonally forward with mandatory jumps and multi-captures, while kings move and capture one step diagonally in any direction.

Move format is a from-to coordinate pair for a single step. I'm uncertain how the engine handles multi-jumps: since captures are mandatory, if a partial jump leaves further captures available for that same piece, I need to continue with it, but without knowing exactly how the engine tracks the jumping piece, there's risk of ambiguity if multiple capture options exist across different pieces.

I could keep track between calls by remembering the board state right after my own first jump segment — if the next state matches that (meaning the opponent hasn't moved yet), I know I'm mid-multi-jump and should continue with the same piece rather than picking a fresh capture elsewhere.

I should also decide on conventions I can't verify directly: whether promotion ends a jump sequence immediately or lets it continue, whether kings fly across multiple squares (international-style) or move like standard English draughts kings, and how the board's dark/light squares and movement directions map to coordinates. I'll go with the standard English checkers ruleset as the safest default, deriving direction and color logic from the piece positions rather than assuming a fixed origin square.

Now I'm worried about mandatory-capture generation being correct, since returning a non-capture when a capture exists (or vice versa under different backward-capture assumptions) would get me disqualified -- I'll commit to forward-only captures for men and any-direction for kings, matching typical English draughts implementations, while noting the ambiguity around backward captures for men as a residual risk.

I'm sketching the engine architecture: representing the board as a flat 64-length array with signed integers for man/king ownership, defining forward direction and promotion rows per color, and planning an alpha-beta search with iterative deepening under a time budget, paired with a material-plus-positional evaluation function. Now I'm working through move generation, particularly how to build complete multi-jump capture sequences without enforcing a maximum-capture rule, consistent with standard English checkers.

For handling promotions mid-jump, I'm implementing the rule that a man's capture sequence ends immediately upon reaching the king row. Since the engine returns one move segment at a time, I need a state-matching trick: storing the expected intermediate board (with and without the captured piece removed) after that segment, so on the next call I can compare the actual board state against these stored versions to detect whether we're continuing the same multi-jump sequence.

If a match is found, I'll just restrict the search to captures available to the piece that just landed, rather than trying to force the exact continuation of my originally planned sequence -- simpler and handles both engine conventions reasonably well. There's an edge case where an engine might represent the whole multi-jump as a single from/final-to move, which my segment-based approach can't fully cover, but most engines seem to expect one-step-at-a-time segments, so I'll go with that.

For the actual search, I'm settling on negamax with alpha-beta pruning, iterative deepening, and time checks, ordering captures first since they're forced when available.

Since captures are forced in checkers, I'll extend the search depth at leaf nodes whenever captures are still available rather than cutting off abruptly, which naturally stays bounded since captures reduce material. For evaluation I'm scoring man pieces at 100 and kings at 160, adding a small bonus for advancement toward the back rank, and thinking about whether to reward keeping men on the back row for defense.

I'm also considering endgame-specific heuristics: when few pieces remain and one side has an advantage, I want to reward reducing the distance between kings so the winning side actively chases down the opponent's pieces, while skipping mobility and trapped-piece detection for now since they're too costly to compute. Starting to write the actual code now, beginning with board indexing setup.

Writing move generation logic...

Still writing jump logic...

Now I'm writing a function to apply a move by copying the board, clearing captured squares, and promoting the piece if it lands on the promotion row. Then I start sketching the negamax search that generates moves for the side to move and handles the no-moves terminal case.

I'm thinking through side-specific move direction and promotion row parameters, plus a time-control scheme that checks elapsed nodes periodically and uses iterative deepening so I can always fall back on the best move from the last fully completed depth, with an early return if there's only one legal move at the root. Then I move into writing the evaluation function that loops over all squares and scores material and positional factors.

Continuing that, I'm precomputing piece-square tables for my men, opponent men, and kings—rewarding advancement, central control, and back-rank presence—then summing these lookups for a fast evaluation, and adding an endgame-aware heuristic. I'm also building in a "trade when ahead" bias so that when I have a material edge, the evaluation nudges toward simplifying the position by scaling the advantage based on how few pieces remain on the board.

I'll only compute the king-chase bonus in sparse endgame positions to save time, and skip a transposition table for simplicity, relying instead on capture-first move ordering and a lightweight killer-move heuristic. Given Python's speed, I'm estimating something like 20-40k nodes/sec, giving a midgame search depth around 6-7.

For the time budget, I'll cap total execution near 0.75 seconds, checking elapsed time every 512 nodes. To handle mid-jump calls from the engine, I'll track the expected board state after a partial capture sequence and compare it against the actual board, ignoring piece-type differences at the landing square in case of promotion, then continue generating captures for that piece as needed.

If the boards match exactly on our turn, that must mean we're mid-jump since the opponent couldn't have replayed the same position in one ply — so I check for further captures from the landing piece and only fall back to a full search if none exist. The tricky part is conventions where captured pieces remain on the board temporarily, since my capture generator might try to illegally re-jump an already-captured piece that I have no other way of identifying except through stored move history.

I'll pass a set of already-captured squares into the jump generator so it can exclude them, building a `piece_captures` function that takes the board, square, side, and this "dead" set. I also need to set up direction constants based on color — black moves toward lower rows, white toward higher — and define promotion rows accordingly, plus handle the edge case of returning a dummy move if no legal moves exist since the game would already be over. Now I'm setting up the time budget and starting to write the core search code.

Writing board representation and move generation...

Still checking quiet moves and confirming the piece-ownership logic is sound before moving to the jump-generation helper.

For mid-jump handling, I'll reuse the jump function by seeding captured squares and taking just the next step, keeping it simple rather than building a separate path tracker.

Now I'm writing the search function with alpha-beta pruning, node counting, timeout checks, and depth-based cutoffs that extend search when captures are available.

For move ordering I'm adding killer move heuristics per ply, moving previously successful moves to the front of the list since moves are comparable tuples. Evaluation will be computed from a fixed perspective and flipped by side multiplier, and I'll build the piece-square table per call based on color, rewarding advancement toward the back row.

For kings I'll add a center bonus and penalize edge placement slightly. In endgames with few pieces left, I want kings to actively close distance on opponent pieces when ahead in material, scoring by Chebyshev distance. At the root, I'll run iterative deepening with move ordering from prior iterations, stopping on timeout, and return just the first step of the best move sequence found.

For multi-jump moves, I should predict the resulting board state after each capture segment—removing the captured piece, placing the moving piece at its destination, and handling promotion—so I can verify the opponent's continuation matches what I expect, since some rule variants let jumps continue after promotion.

I'll pick the best branch by choosing the longest capture path, or better, reuse the root search function to evaluate these candidate moves as if they were root moves, applying a time budget of about 0.8 seconds. Now I'm setting up the core constants and direction tables needed for the full implementation.

Setting up move directions and evaluation tables...

Still writing evaluation loop...

Writing move application and root search logic...

I add a break condition once alpha hits near-mate bounds, since deeper search is pointless there, and otherwise catch timeouts to stop iterating. I'm double-checking the aspiration window logic at the root—using -alpha as beta is correct for the first move, though it sacrifices some move-ordering info on fail-lows, which seems acceptable. I also confirm that a no-move state correctly scores as a loss for the side to move, and now I'm considering whether to add depth extensions on captures.

I need to cap recursion depth so capture chains don't run forever, so I'm adding a ply limit that forces an evaluation once ply reaches 60, while confirming that at depth zero we still search all forced captures. I'm also setting up periodic node-count checks and a killer-move table indexed by ply, moving stored killers to the front of the quiet-move list on beta cutoffs to improve ordering, accepting the linear-scan cost as a reasonable tradeoff.

Now I'm estimating raw performance—roughly 15-25k nodes per second scanning the 64-square board for move generation and evaluation—which should support depth 6-7 search within the time budget, and considering whether piece lists would speed things up but deciding to keep the simpler board-scan approach for now. I'm starting to write the main policy function, setting up the time deadline and board state, then checking whether the last move left the position mid-jump so the agent can continue a forced capture sequence.

Writing mid-jump detection logic...

Then I fall back to standard move generation if no mid-jump is pending, running root search over all legal moves and returning the finishing move—falling back to a placeholder move if none exist, which seems like an edge case I should double check. I also want to verify that captured pieces marked "dead" during a jump sequence are properly excluded from the opponent's subsequent move generation once the move is finalized and applied, since the dead tuple gets passed through the jump search and needs to align with how apply() strips those pieces from the board.

Writing the finish function logic...

I'm double-checking that the dead-piece tracking persists correctly through multi-jump captures, and confirming the root search will apply the correct move convention when it reads these board states.

I also want to verify edge cases: stale LAST data across game restarts shouldn't cause false matches since it requires an identical board, killer move list size is set to 128 plies, and the forward direction/promotion row logic for each color checks out against the PST evaluation table.

For the endgame chase heuristic when material is low, I'm adding logic that pushes the leading side's kings toward the trailing side's pieces by penalizing distance — for this I need to collect all squares belonging to both sides upfront so I can compute the Chebyshev distance between the leading side's kings and any opposing piece.

No mobility loss and tie-breaking concerns are already handled elsewhere, and jump generation for kings versus men looks consistent with the direction tables, with finite recursion guaranteed since each capture step removes a piece. Now I'm writing the main search function, starting with the base case handling and state setup...

Writing search recursion...

I'm also noting to avoid dict overhead for node counting by using globals instead, and setting the time budget to roughly 0.8 seconds out of the 1 second allowed, accounting for Python startup overhead.

The node-check interval of 2048 is too coarse given typical search speeds—checking every 256 nodes gives better timing granularity without adding much overhead. I also confirm the evaluation function's division logic handles edge cases correctly since total material is always positive when moves exist. This looks ready to finalize.
